scenes.title: Position by distance and angle
lines: How should we describe a bullet spreading outward, or an object circling a center?
We will learn polar coordinates: a way to describe position using distance and angle.
First we will observe real gameplay, then locate a point, and finally convert it into horizontal and vertical coordinates.
Let's start by thinking about one bullet's direction and distance.

scenes.title: Gameplay · locating a bullet
lines: This is Enter the Gungeon. Turning the gun changes the direction of the outgoing shots.
Pick one bullet. In which direction, and how far, has it traveled from where it was fired?
We could describe its horizontal and vertical displacement, but direction and distance can locate it too.

scenes.title: Turn, then move forward
lines: Start at the origin facing right. Turn counterclockwise through an angle, then move in that direction.
The point four units right and three units up is five units away, at an angle of about thirty-seven degrees.
We call the distance r and the angle theta. The point stays the same; only its description changes.
Keep the distance fixed and vary the angle. The point traces a circle around the center.

scenes.title: Gameplay · spreading bullets
lines: Watch the boss's red projectiles. They spread in several directions and travel away from their firing point.
To design a motion like this, imagine choosing each bullet's direction, then increasing its distance.
Differences in direction shape the spread; the rate of increasing distance determines how fast the bullets travel.

scenes.title: Convert to x and y
lines: How do we recover the horizontal and vertical coordinates needed to draw the point?
In this right triangle, the hypotenuse is five, the horizontal side is four, and the vertical side is three.
Cosine is horizontal length divided by hypotenuse; sine is vertical length divided by hypotenuse.
Multiply by the distance: horizontal length is r times cosine, and vertical length is r times sine.
Angle units differ. Make sure to distinguish degrees from radians when using them.

scenes.title: Gameplay · a moving center
lines: Notice that the firing character moves too. The center is not always the screen origin.
The lengths we calculated are offsets from the center. Add the firing position to obtain the final coordinates.
We are interpreting visible motion with our coordinate model, rather than claiming to know this game's implementation.

scenes.title: A 3D extension and recap
lines: On the plane, a point keeps its distance while its angle changes. Add height to extend the idea into cylindrical coordinates.
Tilting the space makes it easier to see that rotation and height can be controlled separately.
Remember this: polar coordinates describe how far a position is from a center, and in which direction.
Thinking about the same position in distance and angle makes circular and spreading motion easier to design.
